questions.text:
Let [latex]P[/latex] be the set of all integers from [latex]1[/latex] to [latex]15[/latex]. Consider any order of insertion of the elements of [latex]P[/latex] into a binary search tree that creates a complete binary tree.

Which one of the following elements can NEVER be the third element that is inserted?
questions.solution:
Since the [latex]15[/latex] elements form a complete binary tree that is also a valid BST, the shape and contents of every position are fully determined: the tree must be a perfectly balanced BST on [latex]\{1,\ldots,15\}[/latex]:

Level 0 (root): [latex]8[/latex]
Level 1: [latex]4,\ 12[/latex]
Level 2: [latex]2,\ 6,\ 10,\ 14[/latex]
Level 3 (leaves): [latex]1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15[/latex]

For an insertion sequence to build up exactly this shape via ordinary BST insertion, a node can only be inserted after its parent has already been inserted (a node's tree position is only "unlocked" once its parent exists). So valid insertion orders are precisely the orders in which every node appears after its parent (a topological/level-respecting order).

The root [latex]8[/latex] must always be inserted first. The second insertion must be one of the root's children, [latex]4[/latex] or [latex]12[/latex]. The third insertion can then be: the other level-1 node ([latex]12[/latex] or [latex]4[/latex]), or a level-2 child of whichever level-1 node was inserted second (e.g. [latex]2[/latex] or [latex]6[/latex] if [latex]4[/latex] went second). This gives possible third elements [latex]\{2,4,6,10,12,14\}[/latex] — only levels 0-2 nodes can ever appear as early as the third insertion.

[latex]5[/latex] is a level-3 leaf (child of [latex]6[/latex], which is itself a level-2 child of [latex]4[/latex]). Before [latex]5[/latex] can be inserted, both its ancestors [latex]8[/latex] and [latex]4[/latex] and [latex]6[/latex] would already need to exist — requiring at least [latex]4[/latex] prior insertions. So [latex]5[/latex] can never be inserted as early as third.

Answer: 5 can NEVER be the third element inserted.

We want a recursive count of nodes in a non-empty singly linked list.

The natural recursive base case is: if the current node is the last node (i.e. [latex]\text{head->next==NULL}[/latex]), then this contributes exactly [latex]1[/latex] to the count, so [latex]\text{E1: head->next==NULL}[/latex], returning [latex]1[/latex].

Otherwise, the count is [latex]1[/latex] (for the current node) plus however many nodes remain in the rest of the list starting from [latex]\text{head->next}[/latex]: [latex]\text{E2: 1+getListSize(head->next)}[/latex].

(Using [latex]\text{head==NULL}[/latex] as the base case instead would also work logically for a possibly-empty list, but here the function is documented to be called only on a non-empty list, and combined with the given E2 form, the option that consistently checks [latex]\text{head->next}[/latex] in the base case and recurses on [latex]\text{head->next}[/latex] is the matching, correct pair.)

Answer: E1: head->next == NULL, E2: 1 + getListSize(head->next)

questions.text: The height of a binary tree is the number of edges in the longest path from the root to a leaf in the tree. The maximum possible height of a full binary tree with [latex]23[/latex] nodes is ________.(answer in integer)
questions.solution:
In a full binary tree, every node has either [latex]0[/latex] or [latex]2[/latex] children. If there are [latex]I[/latex] internal (2-children) nodes and [latex]L[/latex] leaves, then [latex]L=I+1[/latex], and total nodes [latex]N=I+L=2I+1[/latex].

For [latex]N=23[/latex]: [latex]23=2I+1\Rightarrow I=11[/latex] internal nodes and [latex]L=12[/latex] leaves.

To maximize height, make the tree as "skewed"/chain-like as possible while still keeping every internal node's 2-children rule: each internal node (except the last one in the chain) has one leaf child and one internal child continuing the chain; the very last internal node has two leaf children.

This chain uses exactly [latex]I=11[/latex] internal nodes along the main path, with the deepest leaves appearing right after the [latex]11[/latex]th internal node. So the longest root-to-leaf path has [latex]11[/latex] edges.

Answer: 11

questions.text:
Consider a hash table [latex]P[0,1, \ldots, 10][/latex] that is initially empty. The hash table is maintained using open addressing with linear probing. The hash function used is [latex]h(x)=(x+7) \bmod 11[/latex].

Consider the following sequence of insertions performed on [latex]P[/latex] :

[latex] \text { 1,13, 22, 15, 11, } 24 [/latex]

Which of the following positions in the hash table is/are empty after these insertions are performed?
questions.solution:
Hash function: [latex]h(x)=(x+7)\bmod 11[/latex], table size [latex]11[/latex] (indices [latex]0[/latex] to [latex]10[/latex]), linear probing.

Compute initial hash and, on collision, probe the next slot(s) circularly:
[latex]\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{Key}&h(x)&\text{Placed at}\\\hline 1&8&8\ (\text{empty})\\13&9&9\ (\text{empty})\\22&7&7\ (\text{empty})\\15&0&0\ (\text{empty})\\11&7&7\text{ taken}\to8\text{ taken}\to9\text{ taken}\to10\ (\text{empty})\\24&9&9\text{ taken}\to10\text{ taken}\to0\text{ taken}\to1\ (\text{empty})\end{array}[/latex]

Final table: [latex]0{:}15,\ 1{:}24,\ 7{:}22,\ 8{:}1,\ 9{:}13,\ 10{:}11[/latex]. Positions [latex]2,3,4,5,6[/latex] remain empty.

Of the choices given (0, 10, 2, 1), only position 2 is empty — the others (0, 1, 10) are all occupied.

Answer: Position 2

questions.text:
Let [latex]n[/latex] be an odd number greater than [latex]100[/latex]. Consider a binary minheap with [latex]n[/latex] elements stored in an array [latex]P[/latex] whose index starts from [latex]1[/latex].
Which of the following indices of [latex]P[/latex] do/does NOT correspond to any leaf node of the minheap?
questions.solution:
In a 1-indexed array representation of a binary heap with [latex]n[/latex] elements, the leaf nodes are exactly the indices [latex]\left\lfloor \dfrac{n}{2}\right\rfloor+1[/latex] through [latex]n[/latex] (nodes with no children).

For odd [latex]n[/latex], [latex]\left\lfloor n/2\right\rfloor=\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex], so:
- Leaf indices: [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}+1=\dfrac{n+1}{2}[/latex] up to [latex]n[/latex].
- Internal (non-leaf) indices: [latex]1[/latex] up to [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex].

Checking the given indices:
- [latex]\dfrac{n+1}{2}[/latex]: this is the first leaf index — corresponds to a leaf.
- [latex]n[/latex]: this is the last leaf — corresponds to a leaf.
- [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex]: this is the last internal node index — it does NOT correspond to a leaf.
- [latex]\dfrac{n-3}{2}[/latex]: this is less than [latex]\dfrac{n-1}{2}[/latex], so also an internal node — does NOT correspond to a leaf.

Answer: indices (n-1)/2 and (n-3)/2 do NOT correspond to leaf nodes.
